aiMessages.say:
Konnichiwa, Tester-san! I am Hana-sensei, and my little calico kitten, Mikan, is curled up beside us, ready to learn too. Let's start from the very beginning.

Imagine a cell is like a cozy little room. Around every cell is a flexible outer barrier called the **cell membrane**. Think of it like the skin or the walls of that room—it holds the cell together and protects the inside from the outside w

Exactly—without that wall, everything inside would spill out!

Now, what makes up this barrier? It's mostly built from special fats called **phospholipids**.

Instead of just one sheet, these molecules form two layers that face each other. We call this a **bilayer**—just like *bicycle* means two wheels, *bilayer* means two layers. You can imagine it like two slices of bread making a sandwich aroun

Daijoubu (it's okay), Tester-san! It's an easy mix-up when we are starting out.

While cells do have proteins, the main blanket wrapping the cell is made of fatty molecules called **phospholipids**. 

Because there are two layers pressed together, we use the prefix **bi-** (just like *bi*cycle has two wheels). Putting those two words together gives us the name for this double layer.

Let's try tha

Yatta! (You did it!) That is exactly right.

So, every living cell is wrapped in this special **phospholipid bilayer**. It acts like a flexible, protective skin, keeping the watery contents inside safe from the watery environment outside.

Mikan gives you a gentle paw of approval! Let's do one last check to make sure this foundational idea is crystal clear.

Subarashii! (Wonderful!) You have mastered our very first goal: the cell membrane is a protective barrier made of a **phospholipid bilayer**.

Mikan is purring happily right beside your notes. You are officially one step closer to passing your biology class!

Whenever you are ready, we will dive into Lesson 2 to see the fascinating heads and tails of these phospholipids. Great work today!

lessons.title: Introduction to Cell Membranes
lessons.goal: Understand the basic phospholipid bilayer structure of the cell membrane.

lessons.title: Phospholipid Heads and Tails
lessons.goal: Learn the difference between hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails.

lessons.title: The Fluid Mosaic Model
lessons.goal: Explain how floating proteins create the fluid mosaic structure.

lessons.title: Integral Membrane Proteins
lessons.goal: Identify how integral proteins span the membrane to serve as channels or carriers.

lessons.title: Peripheral Membrane Proteins
lessons.goal: Explore how peripheral proteins sit on membrane surfaces as enzymes or signals.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates and the Glycocalyx
lessons.goal: Understand how carbohydrate chains attached to proteins enable cell recognition.

lessons.title: Selective Permeability Basics
lessons.goal: Define selective permeability and how membranes regulate crossing molecules.

lessons.title: Diffusion of Small Nonpolar Molecules
lessons.goal: Learn how oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse freely across the bilayer.

lessons.title: Transport of Ions and Polar Molecules
lessons.goal: Understand why ions and large polar molecules require transport proteins.

lessons.title: Osmosis and Water Concentration
lessons.goal: Explain how water diffuses across membranes from low to high solute concentration.

cards.front: What is the primary structure of the cell membrane?
cards.back: The cell membrane is arranged as a phospholipid bilayer.

cards.front: What are the two main regions of a phospholipid?
cards.back: Each phospholipid has one hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails.

cards.front: Where do phospholipid heads face in water?
cards.back: The hydrophilic heads face outward toward the surrounding water.

cards.front: Where do phospholipid tails point in water?
cards.back: The hydrophobic tails hide inside the bilayer, away from water.

cards.front: Why is the membrane structure called a mosaic?
cards.back: It is called a mosaic because proteins float within the lipid bilayer like icebergs.

cards.front: What role do proteins play in the fluid mosaic model?
cards.back: Proteins float inside the phospholipid bilayer.

cards.front: How many tails does each membrane phospholipid have?
cards.back: Each phospholipid has two hydrophobic tails.

cards.front: What is the name of the model describing membrane structure?
cards.back: It is called the fluid mosaic model.
